body.text: A much-weaker-than-expected US jobs report, coupled with downward revisions of early jobs growth, wound back expectations of a rate rise from the Fed this month and boosted Wall Street stocks after a turbulent week.
The ASX looks like maintaining its momentum from Friday with futures trading pointing to a gain on opening.

Is the bond market rout overdone?
Capital Economics markets strategy team posted an interesting note asking the question "was the bond market rout" — that is, falling bond prices and rising interest rates — "overdone?"
"Perhaps" seems to be the answer, but that doesn't mean equity markets are about to be given a leg up if interest rates stop rising and edge lower.
Quite the opposite, according to Capital Economics (CE), which sees see the AI-driven equity rally as bubble waiting to burst.

CE noted that markets in the past quarter have been dominated by three stories that have been important all year: the waxing and waning of investors' enthusiasm for AI-exposed equities, big swings in commodity prices, and a sharp rise in bond yields.
"We think all three trends are approaching turning points," CE's Chief Markets Economist Jonas Goltermann wrote in a note.
"We suspect the AI-driven equity rally has become stretched and will turn into a rout at some point.
"We also expect commodity prices to fall back, with the caveat that energy prices will continue to depend heavily on developments in the Strait of Hormuz.
"And we think that government bonds will recover as tightening cycles underwhelm expectations."
On the bond rout, Mr Goltermann expects a reversal before too long.

"We expect the sell-off in DM (Developed Market) government bonds to unwind over the coming year or so as energy prices drop back and most central banks tighten policy by less than is now discounted, generating good returns from bonds.

"We think corporate bond spreads will widen markedly given our view that the AI stock market boom will turn to bust, especially given that huge AI-related bond issuance has increased the direct exposure of that asset class to AI."
CE's view is that the AI boom's day of reckoning may be sooner rather than later.

"While timing such crashes is hard, our forecasts envisage one happening next year. That allows for the possibility of a final 'blow-off' phase in which tech stocks, in particular, make further gains before heading sharply lower."
Key Event
OPEC+ agrees to keep November oil output targets steady

OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday.

Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the US-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.

"The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said."Consequently, the oil market remains tight."

"Consequently, the oil market remains tight."

Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to US President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $US100 a barrel, up from about $US73 before the Iran war started in late February.

The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members' 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.

Key Event
Calling AI 'other intelligence' better describes the advent of a new lifeform
Finance guru Alan Kohler says humanity has essentially created a new lifeform in the form of artificial intelligence (AI).
In his latest column, Alan wrote:

The hack of Medicare by an OpenAI agent, which followed other hacks by AI agents, illuminated the fact that these companies are not building a screwdriver that exists only as a tool for humans; they're building agents that turn passive AI into active autonomy.
And cyber security experts I've spoken to tell me we are rapidly approaching a situation where only autonomous AI agents will be able to defend against other autonomous AI agents.

The use of AI by agents — that is the buying of tokens from large language models (LLMs) — went past human usage by volume in February and has since increased 14-fold while human token buying has merely tripled, according to Open Router, an LLM marketplace.
Agents now use five times as much AI as humans and that gap is continuing to widen rapidly.

It's a very quiet week data-wise ahead.
Locally, the only numbers of note will be Westpac-MI consumer sentiment index (Tuesday) which will tell us again that we are deeply pessimistic (sigh).
The Fed releases the minutes from its FOMC meeting where interest rates were raised last month (Thursday).

The latest Fed communications have been along the lines of there's no need for urgency in further rate hikes, the minutes are likely to be more of the same, but there may be hints about whether more needs to be done to quell inflation.
Key Event
Wall Street gains on weak jobs data, ASX priced to rise
After a bumpy week Wall Street closed with a mini rally on Friday, although it was inspired, in part, by some less-than-stellar economic news.
• Nasdaq: +1.2%
US non-farm payrolls gained a much weaker than expected 29,000 jobs in September. Market observers had pencilled in a gain of 90,000.
Compounding September's labour market softness was a severe downward revision of jobs growth over the previous two months before that.
The weaker-than-anticipated data pulled down expectations for a rate hike of at least 25 basis points from the Fed at its meeting at the end of October to around 23 from 64% a week earlier.
"Today's news was OK insofar as it means the economy isn't roaring," SummitTX Capital head of trading Robert Bernstone told Reuters.

"But how good is that? Yes, it's fine insofar as it takes the short-term rate hike off, but there is a concern over the economy, there is a concern over inflation, so cautious optimism is kind of where people are."
"But with that said, a potential squeeze into the end of the year, or at least for the next month or two, could happen just because it's a hated rally."
US tech rally

Tempered expectations for an impending rate hike helped boost rate-sensitive stocks such as the S&P 500 real estate index, which gained 0.4%, and the small-cap Russell 2000 index, which gained 0.9% to register its biggest daily gain in a month.
Mega-cap stocks helped lead the advance, with Nvidia up 1.3% and Tesla gaining 4.7% to put them among the biggest boosts to the S&P 500.
Despite Friday's gains, both the Dow and S&P 500 recorded a fourth weekly decline in the past five, but the Nasdaq secured a weekly gain, its fifth in the last six.
For the week, the S&P 500 shed 0.3%, the Nasdaq rose 0.5%, and the Dow fell 1.3%.
ASX to open higher
It might not feel like it, but the ASX 200 still managed to gain 0.2% over the week despite Thursday's 2% stumble.
Futures trading points to the ASX 200 gaining 0.3% this morning.
US Treasury yields continued to edge higher despite the poor job numbers.
The yield on benchmark US 10-year note rose 2.8 basis points to 5.26%.

The 30-year bond yield rose 1.76 basis points to 5.62%, and the 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Federal Reserve, rose 3.14 basis points to 4.81%.
Despite the Greenback's rise, the Aussie dollar made gains against it, up 0.3% to 69.53 US cents.
The global oil benchmark Brent crude future was pretty flat, still holding above $US100/barrel. The US benchmark WTI crude futures fell 2%.
Gold lost ground on the session (-0.9% to $US4,142/ounce) and over the week on the back of a stronger US dollar.
Copper slipped on a soft turnover but is still around 16% higher over the past 6 months.

It may be a public holiday across large swathes of the nation, but not on the ASX, nor here in the ABC Business Unit's Room 101 where we will be hard at work sifting the truths from the untruths.
Wall Street closed the week higher with weaker than expected jobs data chilling expectations of another rate rise from the Fed this month.
The ASX looks to have regained a bit of its mojo. Futures trading, at the close on Saturday morning (AEST), pointed to a 0.3% gain today following Friday's 0.8% rally.
It's a quietish day on the data front with only the Inflation Gauge and S&P Global's Australian services PMI set for release.
Anyway, the game's afoot, so let's get blogging.
